title: Project roles: users, team, board & product owner
blurb: Know what users, team members, the project manager, the steering group/board and the product owner each do, and explain why the roles are kept distinct.
question: A housing association is building an online portal for tenants. The finance director is sponsor, an IT supplier is building it in two-week iterations, and a tenant liaison officer will decide what gets built next. Who sits on the project board, what does each role do, and why does it matter that their responsibilities are kept separate?

teach.body: A project's roles are the defined set of responsibilities and authority that each person or group holds in the temporary project organisation. The core roles are the sponsor, the steering group or board, the project manager, project team members and users, plus a product owner in iterative work. Plain English: someone sets the direction, someone runs the project day to day, someone does the work, and someone will use the result. Writing those jobs down stops gaps, overlaps and arguments later.

teach.caption: Users are represented on the board by the senior user, and work with the team on requirements and testing.
The heart of role design: those who direct are kept separate from the one who manages and those who deliver.

head: Role
Key responsibilities
rows: Set requirements, test, accept, adopt outputs, realise benefits
Deliver work packages, specialist input, estimates, progress
Plan, lead, control, report; escalate beyond tolerance
Direction, gate decisions, escalations, commit resources
Owns and prioritises backlog; accepts work each iteration
teach.caption: The sponsor chairs the board, owns the business case and is accountable for the benefits.

teach.h: Why the roles are kept distinct
teach.body: Distinct roles give clear accountability: one named owner for each decision. They separate DIRECTION (sponsor and board) from MANAGEMENT (project manager) and DELIVERY (team), so the people judging progress are not marking their own homework. They avoid gaps and duplicated effort, make sure decisions are taken at the right level, and build the users' voice into the project. Unclear roles lead to slow decisions, duplicated work and outputs nobody wanted.

teach.h: Inside the steering group or board
teach.body: The board is chaired by the sponsor and usually includes a senior user (speaking for those who will use the outputs) and a senior supplier (speaking for those who will build them). Its job is direction, not daily management: approving plans, making go/no-go decisions at gates, resolving issues the project manager escalates, and committing the resources the project needs. A board that meets only when things go wrong is reacting, not directing.

teach.h: Roles in linear and iterative life cycles

teach.body: The finance director is sponsor and chairs a board with the head of tenant services (senior user) and the supplier's account director (senior supplier). The project manager plans the release, manages the budget and reports monthly. Developers and testers are team members. A tenant liaison officer is product owner: she ranks the backlog and accepts each iteration's features. Tenants are the users: a panel tests every iteration, and their adoption of the portal will realise the benefits.

teach.text: The product owner is NOT the project manager. The product owner represents the business, owns and prioritises the backlog and accepts the work. The project manager plans, controls and reports. Also beware options that treat users as passive recipients: users define requirements, test, accept and adopt.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name each role the question lists and give one or two clear responsibilities.
Separate direction (sponsor, board) from management (PM) and delivery (team).
Explain why distinct roles help: accountability, right-level decisions, no gaps.
Mention the product owner where the life cycle is iterative.
Apply it to the scenario: who should decide the problem described?
Users: requirements, testing, acceptance, adoption and benefits.
Team members: deliver work packages, specialist input, estimates, progress.
Project manager: day-to-day planning, control, leadership and reporting.
Board: sponsor plus senior user and senior supplier; direction and decisions.
Product owner: owns and prioritises the backlog; accepts work each iteration.

summary: You can now state the responsibilities of users, team members, the project manager, the steering group or board and the product owner. You can also explain why separating direction, management and delivery gives clear accountability and better decisions.

A.q: On an iterative project, which role owns and prioritises the product backlog?
A.why: The product owner represents the business, owns the backlog and decides its priority order.

whyNot.0: The project manager plans, controls and reports; prioritising the backlog belongs to the product owner.
whyNot.1: The senior supplier represents those building the solution on the board.
whyNot.3: Team members deliver items from the backlog; they do not own its priorities.

A.q: Which of the following is a core responsibility of the USERS on a project?
options: Chairing the board and owning the business case
Allocating daily tasks to the project team
A.why: Users help define requirements, test and accept the outputs, then adopt them so the benefits are realised.

whyNot.1: Chairing the board and owning the business case is the sponsor's role.
whyNot.2: The project manager produces the project management plan.
whyNot.3: Allocating day-to-day work is the project manager's job.

A.q: Who typically makes up a project steering group or board?
options: The PM and all of the project team members
Users only, chaired by the PMO lead
Supplier staff and the project team
A.why: The board is chaired by the sponsor with senior user and senior supplier representatives, so business, user and supplier views shape decisions.

whyNot.0: The PM and team manage and deliver; they are not the board that directs them.
whyNot.1: The board needs the sponsor and supplier view too, and the PMO supports rather than chairs it.
whyNot.2: This leaves out the sponsor and the users' voice.

B.q: What is the MAIN reason for keeping project roles distinct?
options: To reduce the number of meetings held
To give each decision a clear owner
To let the PM approve the business case
To keep users away from the project team
B.why: Distinct roles give each decision a clear owner and separate direction from management and delivery.

whyNot.0: Fewer meetings may follow, but it is not the purpose.
whyNot.2: The sponsor owns and approves the business case, not the PM.
whyNot.3: Users should work closely with the team on requirements and testing.

B.q: Which responsibility belongs to PROJECT TEAM MEMBERS?
options: Accepting the outputs on behalf of users
B.why: Team members deliver the work packages, bring specialist expertise, give estimates and report progress to the PM.

whyNot.0: Committing funding at gates is a board and sponsor decision.
whyNot.1: Acceptance is for users (or the product owner in iterative work).
whyNot.2: Benefits after handover are the sponsor's accountability, with users and business managers.

B.q: A board member starts giving developers their daily task lists, bypassing the project manager. Which principle of role design is MOST undermined?
options: Basing decisions on the business case
B.why: The board directs; the project manager manages day to day. A board member allocating tasks blurs that line and undermines the PM's authority.

whyNot.1: User representation is about the senior user's role, not task allocation.
whyNot.2: Backlog prioritisation is a product owner matter, not the issue here.
whyNot.3: The problem is who is directing the team, not the basis of the decision.

C.q: Midway through a two-week iteration on a ticketing app, the marketing team asks for a new discount feature. Who should decide whether it goes into the next iteration?
options: The developer who would build it
The board, through formal change control
The project manager, on the PM's own view
C.why: In iterative work most scope changes are absorbed by the product owner reprioritising the backlog between iterations.

whyNot.0: Developers estimate and build; they do not decide business priority.
whyNot.1: Formal change control is kept for changes to the fixed time, cost or overall objectives.
whyNot.3: The PM facilitates; prioritising backlog items is the product owner's responsibility.

C.q: Which TWO are responsibilities of the steering group or board? 1. Decisions at gates  2. Writing work package estimates  3. Committing resources  4. Allocating daily tasks
C.why: The board gives direction: it makes go/no-go decisions at gates and commits the resources the project needs.

whyNot.0: Writing work package estimates is for team members.
whyNot.2: Estimates and daily task allocation are delivery and management jobs.
whyNot.3: Allocating daily tasks is the project manager's job.

C.q: A council's new parking permit system meets its specification, but residents reject it at go-live because it does not fit how they apply. What is the MOST likely cause in role terms?
options: The sponsor did not chair the board
The PMO did not set reporting standards
The team did not give progress reports
Users were not involved in requirements
C.why: Users should help set requirements and test outputs. Leaving them out until go-live is the classic cause of outputs that meet a specification but fail in use.

whyNot.0: Who chairs the board does not explain why the design missed the users' needs.
whyNot.1: Reporting standards affect consistency, not whether the solution fits users.
whyNot.2: Missing progress reports cause control problems, not a mismatch with user needs.

reteach.title: Building a house extension
reteach.question: A family is adding a kitchen extension. Who plays the sponsor, the board, the project manager, the team and the users?

blocks.body: The parent paying for it is the sponsor: they decide whether it is worth doing and sign off the money. The family who will cook and eat there are the users: they say what they need and check the result works. The builder's site manager is the project manager, running the job day to day. The bricklayers, plumbers and electricians are the team. A monthly sit-down between the family and the builder's director is the board.

blocks.text: If the paying parent starts telling the electrician where every socket goes each morning, the site manager can no longer manage. That is exactly why direction and management are kept apart.

explain.body: The sponsor chairs the steering group or board, which includes a senior user and a senior supplier. Together they set direction, decide at gates, resolve escalated issues and commit resources. They do not manage the work day to day.

test.q: Who normally chairs the project steering group or board?
test.why: The sponsor chairs the board and is accountable for the business case and benefits.

whyNot.1: The senior user is a board member representing users, not the chair.
whyNot.2: The PMO supports governance but does not chair the board.
whyNot.3: The project manager reports to the board; they are not its chair.

explain.body: The project manager runs the project day to day: planning, leading the team, controlling delivery against the baseline, reporting progress and managing risks and problems within tolerances. Anything forecast to go beyond tolerance is an issue, escalated to the sponsor.

test.q: Which of these is a project manager responsibility?
options: Chairing the board's decision gate reviews
Leading the team and reporting progress
test.why: The PM leads the team, controls delivery and reports progress to the sponsor and board.

whyNot.0: Benefits after closure are the sponsor's accountability.
whyNot.1: Gate decisions are taken by the sponsor and board.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier represents suppliers on the board.

explain.body: Team members deliver work packages, bring specialist knowledge, provide estimates and report progress. Users state requirements, test and accept the outputs, then adopt them so the benefits are realised.

test.q: On a warehouse automation project, who should provide the specialist estimates for the robotics installation work package?
test.why: Team members doing the work have the specialist knowledge to estimate it.

whyNot.0: Users give requirements and test outputs; they don't estimate specialist work.
whyNot.2: The sponsor approves budgets but does not estimate work packages.
whyNot.3: The senior user represents users on the board; estimates come from the team.

explain.body: In iterative life cycles the product owner represents the business, owns and prioritises the backlog, answers the team's questions about what is needed, and accepts the work at the end of each iteration. This keeps decisions about value close to the team.

test.q: At the end of each iteration, what does the product owner typically do?
options: Signs off the PM's monthly timesheets
Reviews and accepts the completed work
test.why: The product owner reviews and accepts the work delivered in each iteration, then reprioritises the backlog for the next.

whyNot.0: The business case is owned and approved at sponsor and board level.
whyNot.1: Tolerances are delegated by the sponsor and board.
whyNot.2: Timesheet approval is an administrative line-management task, not a product owner role.
